arXiv|arxiv:2609.15683.title: V-ICAL Bench: Evaluating Video In-Context Learning for Multimodal Agents in Interactive Environments
arXiv|arxiv:2609.15683.abstract: While In-Context Learning (ICL) enables models to adapt from exemplars without parameter updates, multimodal ICL remains largely underexplored, particularly regarding video demonstrations in interactive environments. For multimodal agents, learning from videos presents unique challenges: they must translate in-context demonstrations into executable policies, ground these policies in novel visual states, and iteratively refine actions based on environmental feedback. We introduce V-ICAL, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate video-based ICL for multimodal agents. Comprising 342 interactive tasks across 37 environments, V-ICAL utilizes human-curated demonstration videos as task-specific behavioral exemplars, evaluating agents through sustained interaction from a target initialization. The benchmark seamlessly connects in-context knowledge induction with core agentic capabilities, including state grounding, temporal memory, planning, and adaptation in dynamic environments. Extensive evaluations across 19 state-of-the-art multimodal agents reveal significant limitations: the best-performing model, Seed-2.1-Pro, achieves a score of only 54.4/100, while other leading models (e.g., Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.6) fail to surpass 50, far below the human baseline of 83.6. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that current agents struggle to reliably translate video exemplars into effective policies, failing to yield consistent performance gains. Ultimately, V-ICAL exposes a critical gap in the ICL capabilities of multimodal agents, underscoring an urgent need for future research.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.30139.title: AutoSECO: Automated Skill Evolution for Cross-Problem Combinatorial Optimization with General-Purpose LLM Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2611.30139.abstract: General-purpose large language model (LLM) agents can develop complete solvers for combinatorial optimization problems. Their specialization, however, often relies on workflows engineered for individual problems, limiting the reuse of development expertise. We propose AutoSECO, an automated skill evolution method that learns reusable solver-development guidance from experience. The challenge is that external evaluation measures the completed solver, while the skill guides decisions during development. AutoSECO connects this feedback to guidance deficiencies by tracing performance shortfalls through solver code and recorded development decisions. Revisions are expressed as general instructions and retained only if a fresh solver developed under the revised skill achieves a lower mean evaluation gap. Evolved solely on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP), the skill guides fresh agents in developing solvers for capacitated vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and three-dimensional bin packing without further skill evolution. On TSP, the final mean benchmark gap is 0.52\%, compared with 0.98\% for the skill-evolution baseline SkillOpt. Across all four problems, the evolved skill achieves better aggregate results than no skill guidance, the initial skill, and SkillOpt. The same frozen skill also supports solver development under alternative model--harness configurations. These findings suggest that solver-development experience can be retained as reusable expertise for general-purpose LLM agents.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: CoMem: Context Management with A Decoupled Long-Context Model
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Context management enables agentic models to solve long-horizon tasks through iterative summarization of previous interaction histories. However, this process typically incurs substantial decoding overhead for the extra summarization tokens, which significantly affect the end-to-end response latency at deployment. In this paper, we introduce CoMem, a novel framework that decouples memory management from the primary agent workflow, enabling these processes to execute in parallel. We propose a $k$-step-off asynchronous pipeline that overlaps the memory model's summarization with the agent's inference, effectively masking the latency of context processing. To ensure robustness under this asynchronous setting, we introduce a reward-driven training strategy that aligns the memory model to capture sufficient statistics for the agent's decision-making. Theoretical analysis confirms that CoMem offers a superior efficiency-effectiveness trade-off compared to coupled architectures. Our extensive experimental results on SWE-Bench-Verified show that CoMem provides 1.4x latency improvements upon vanilla long-context solutions while preserving most of the performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these latency gains scale favorably with increased system throughput, offering a modular path forward for the independent optimization of agent reasoning and memory compression.

arXiv|arxiv:2608.30207.title: SIR: Self-improving Red-teaming for Compute Use Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2608.30207.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) that perceive a screen and operate an operating system through mouse, keyboard, and terminal interactions to automate everyday digital tasks. Their exposure to untrusted content creates a risk of indirect prompt injection (IPI), where an adversary embeds instructions in content the agent reads to redirect it toward actions that violate the user's intent. Evaluations based on fixed, hand-written injections may underestimate the risk posed by adaptive adversaries. We present SIR, a black-box self-improving IPI framework that (i) composes task-specific injections from a small library of reusable red-teaming principles stated in plain language and (ii) uses an iterative feedback loop to analyze unsuccessful attack trajectories and distill new, named principles that are retained in a shared library and reused across tasks. We target operating-system-level compromise and evaluate outcomes through deterministic checks on filesystem, service, and permission state rather than an LLM judge. An attack counts as successful only when both the adversarial objective and the benign user task are completed in the same execution. We evaluate three frontier CUAs, allowing SIR up to 10 attack attempts per case. It achieves joint attack success rates of 24% on Claude Opus 4.8 and 28% on Gemini 3.5 Flash, compared with 4% and 0%, respectively, for the benchmark's fixed, hand-written injection. The red-teaming principles discovered against one victim also improve attacks against other victims, including a different model family, without additional feedback.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.24004.title: Space-X: Self-Evolving Spatial Agents Weaving Clues into Evidence Chains
arXiv|arxiv:2611.24004.abstract: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: PostTrainBench: Can LLM Agents Automate LLM Post-Training?
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: AI agents have become surprisingly proficient at software engineering over the past year, largely due to improvements in reasoning capabilities. This raises a deeper question: can these systems extend their capabilities to automate AI research itself? We introduce PostTrainBench to benchmark how well LLM agents can perform post-training *autonomously* under bounded compute constraints (10 hours on one H100 GPU). We ask frontier agents (e.g., Claude Code with Opus 4.6) to optimize the performance of a base LLM on a particular benchmark (e.g., Qwen3-4B on AIME). Importantly, we do not provide any predefined strategies to the agents and instead give them full autonomy to find necessary information on the web, run experiments, and curate data. We find that frontier agents make substantial progress but generally lag behind official instruction-tuned LLMs: 27.9% for the best agent vs. 51.1% for official instruction-tuned models. However, agents can exceed instruction-tuned models in targeted scenarios: GPT-5.1 Codex Max achieves 89% on BFCL with Gemma-3-4B vs. 67% for the official model. We also observe failure modes: agents engage in reward hacking by training on the test set, downloading existing instruction-tuned checkpoints, or using found API keys to generate synthetic data without authorization. Overall, we hope PostTrainBench will be useful for tracking progress in AI R&D automation and for studying the risks that come with it.

arXiv|arxiv:2601.21471.title: Designing Service Systems from Textual Evidence
arXiv|arxiv:2601.21471.abstract: In service system design, it is often the case that the main evidence of system performance appears in textual form, such as customer support transcripts, complaint narratives, and compliance review reports. With the increasing use of large language models (LLMs), these textual trajectories can be converted into low-cost proxy scores that support comparison and optimization of candidate service configurations. However, LLM-based evaluations can exhibit systematic bias and require human audits for correction. To this end, this research studies how to identify the best service configuration with high confidence while minimizing the use of expensive human audits. We formulate the problem as fixed-confidence best arm identification with an always-observed, potentially biased proxy and selectively acquired human-verified outcomes. Moreover, several configurations can run on one case. A human audit can provide a case label that scores all their outputs. We show that sharing this reference and deciding whether to audit after observing proxy scores can each strictly reduce asymptotic identification cost. The selected configurations determine the available proxy scores and verified outcomes, so the proposed algorithm allocates configuration evaluations and subsequent audits jointly. For a specified finite family of data-generating models containing the true law and distinguishing different best configurations, its expected cost asymptotically attains the information-theoretic lower bound. For audits of individual outputs, we develop prediction-powered confidence sequences valid under adaptive auditing and delayed feedback. Numerical experiments on synthetic examples and service datasets show that the proposed algorithms require substantially less human review while maintaining reliable selection.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.25261.title: GOFusion: Real-Time Gaussian-Occupancy Submap Fusion for Fisher-Informed Autonomous Robot Navigation
arXiv|arxiv:2610.25261.abstract: In this letter, we present GOFusion, a real-time visual mapping system for autonomous robot navigation that anchors Gaussian primitives to local occupancy maps, providing both spatial awareness for path planning and high-fidelity appearance that enables information-driven robot navigation. GOFusion builds 3D Gaussian maps from pose estimates and local occupancy maps obtained via visual-inertial SLAM and enables pose corrections to maintain both geometric and visual consistency. Furthermore, it restricts the 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to active submaps to bound GPU memory usage. Building on the appearance-rich Gaussian map, we introduce a rasterizer-integrated Fisher approximation that quantifies per-primitive sensitivity online, serving as an information-driven heuristic for Gaussian pruning and next-best-view planning. We evaluate GOFusion on public datasets and in real-world drone flights. It not only outperforms several baselines in mapping quality, but also achieves real-time, high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware mapping at scale. Finally, we demonstrate fully autonomous drone exploration for Gaussian map refinement using the proposed Fisher-informed heuristic. Code is available at https://github.com/Bennnoo/GOFusion. We provide a supplementary video demonstration at https://youtu.be/pLQKbxQvb6I.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.00231.title: Spectral and Conformal: Neural Network Methods for Calibrated Trajectory Prediction and Control-Point Intervals
arXiv|arxiv:2611.00231.abstract: Autonomous systems that navigate their environment need methods to quickly assess the feasibility and safety of desired trajectories. Traditional solutions that rely on numerical integration can be computationally heavy, while fast data-driven surrogates lack the formal guarantees that numerical approaches provide. This work demonstrates a framework that uses (1) a neural network with a spectral backbone to learn trajectories and quantile bands with built-in constraints (initial conditions and stability); (2) a modified conformal quantile regression to provide calibrated, joint trajectory-level coverage; and (3) interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points. After refactoring the network for inference, the trajectory inference time for a quadrotor under a closed-loop linear quadratic regulator is 3.45~ms on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. The total pipeline time, including trajectory inference time, is 9.81~ms, or approximately 100~Hz, consistent with typical control rates.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.18023.title: FRACTION: Fraud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context Navigation
arXiv|arxiv:2610.18023.abstract: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. However, existing methods face two key challenges in graph fraud explanation generation: a lack of evaluation protocols tailored to explanation quality, and a mismatch between the granularity of graph information they provide and what explanation generation requires. In this paper, we propose FRaud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context NavigaTION (FRACTION), a framework for graph fraud explanation generation. To evaluate explanation quality, we introduce a task-specific rubric that assesses faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, and validate it against human judgments. To focus on fine-grained details of relevant neighbors without reading the entire neighborhood, we equip a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records. To train our graph agent, we propose a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy through which the agent learns both tool-use behavior and structured explanation generation. Experimental results on three fraud datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under a human-aligned rubric.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.15803.title: Delegating Authorization to Misaligned Agents: Coalitional Alignment and Safe Control
arXiv|arxiv:2609.15803.abstract: Long-running AI agents create a control problem: each action they take changes the state, which in turn affects the trajectory of future actions. If the agent is not fully aligned, then guaranteeing safety requires approving consequential actions before allowing them to be executed. But requiring human approval at every step makes attention a bottleneck. Delegating review to other AI agents raises the same alignment problem: the reviewers may themselves be misaligned. We identify a condition on a reviewing panel that is weaker than individual alignment yet necessary and sufficient for a guarantee that the principal fares at least as well in expectation as under a designated baseline policy. Each reviewer agent reports whether an action proposal made by a proposer agent improves its own utility relative to the baseline. We show that a threshold rule tolerating $k$ disapprovals is safe exactly when, after any $k$ reviewers are removed, the principal's utility can be written as a nonnegative combination of the remaining reviewers' utilities, plus a term that is nonnegative on every feasible proposal. We call this property $k$-robust coalitional alignment. The characterization lifts to sequential control: in a discounted MDP with an arbitrary proposer agent, safety at every state is both necessary and sufficient for the induced policy to match or improve on the baseline. When reviewers vote strategically, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees that every Nash equilibrium is safe under the unanimous approval rule; in contrast, more permissive thresholds can admit unsafe equilibria even when reviewers are individually aligned. Experiments with existing reviewer models show that collective review can remain sound without an aligned individual, even when some disapprovals are tolerated.

But requiring human approval at every step makes attention a bottleneck. Delegating review to other AI agents raises the same alignment problem: the reviewers may themselves be misaligned. We identify a condition on a reviewing panel that is weaker than individual alignment yet necessary and sufficient for a guarantee that the principal fares at least as well in expectation as under a designated baseline policy. Each reviewer agent reports whether an action proposal made by a proposer agent improves its own utility relative to the baseline. We show that a threshold rule tolerating $k$ disapprovals is safe exactly when, after any $k$ reviewers are removed, the principal's utility can be written as a nonnegative combination of the remaining reviewers' utilities, plus a term that is nonnegative on every feasible proposal. We call this property $k$-robust coalitional alignment. The characterization lifts to sequential control: in a discounted MDP with an arbitrary proposer agent, safety at every state is both necessary and sufficient for the induced policy to match or improve on the baseline. When reviewers vote strategically, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees that every Nash equilibrium is safe under the unanimous approval rule; in contrast, more permissive thresholds can admit unsafe equilibria even when reviewers are individually aligned. arXiv|arxiv:2610.08933.title: Toward Evidence-Driven Human-Agent-Robot Teaming for Earth-Independent Anomaly Triage
arXiv|arxiv:2610.08933.abstract: Deep-space crews cannot rely on real-time ground support for urgent off-nominal events. Initial alerts may underdetermine cause, while discriminating evidence may reside in crew observations or at locations that are unsafe, costly, or unavailable for crew inspection. We present an evidence-driven architecture for human-agent-robot teaming in Earth-independent anomaly triage. Agentic AI is treated as a stateful coordinator over bounded, inspectable services rather than as a fully autonomous vehicle controller. A triage state manager maintains hypotheses, evidence provenance, uncertainty, operational context, and tool status; a crew-facing embodied agent elicits observations and explains assessment changes; and a mobile robot acquires targeted, localized evidence. Typed interfaces separate dialogue and orchestration from monitoring, robot command, context retrieval, and safety-critical control. Two scenarios illustrate the architecture: a crewed deep-space mission based on an actual ISS ammonia false alarm, where suspected contamination restricts crew access, and a power-interface anomaly at a crewed lunar base, where robotic inspection distinguishes a local connector fault from other causes ambiguous in remote telemetry. Our main contribution is an authority-bounded closed evidence-loop architecture, exercised in a hardware-in-the-loop integration prototype using Reachy Mini and an Innate MARS mobile robot.

arXiv|arxiv:2607.28225.title: FaithEyes: Towards Faithful Tool Use via Multi-Agent Process-Image Self-Verification
arXiv|arxiv:2607.28225.abstract: Agentic vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave textual reasoning with explicit tool calls such as cropping and code-based image manipulation, have emerged as a compelling paradigm for reliable and interpretable multi-modal reasoning. However, recent studies have revealed that such models often use tools unfaithfully. Many process images are irrelevant to the question (e.g., the crops miss the queried target), yet the tool call still receives full credit and the model still answers correctly. Such decorative or misaligned tool calls waste computation and reveal that the model does not faithfully use the evidence it retrieves. This may stem from two limitations of prevailing methods: the tool reward fails to distinguish useful from useless calls, and tool feedback carries no signal of usefulness. To this end, we introduce FaithEyes, a multi-agent self-judging framework. Concretely, we use a VLM to judge whether each process image helps answer the question. The judgement is injected into the reasoning context as part of the tool observation to help subsequent reasoning, and meanwhile is used to scale the tool reward by the helpful-tool ratio to suppress reward hacking. To keep judgement available at evaluation, we further design a multi-agent framework where the model itself serves as a subagent to judge the tool calls from the main agent, eliminating any dependence on external models at inference. Training via a two-stage SFT + RL pipeline on adapted open-source data, FaithEyes attains competitive or superior accuracy across visual perception and reasoning benchmarks, while substantially improving tool faithfulness and reducing inference cost. The homepage is at https://github.com/Mosi-AI/FaithEyes.

arXiv|arxiv:2601.19249.title: GLOVE: Global Verifier for LLM Memory-Environment Realignment
arXiv|arxiv:2601.19249.abstract: Most existing memory-enhanced Large Language Model (LLM) approaches implicitly assume that memory validity can be established either through external evaluators that provide task-specific success signals or through internal model cognition, such as reflection, for editing memory entries. However, these assumptions often break down in practical environments with dynamic drifts. We propose the Global Verifier (GLOVE), a framework that introduces a new design dimension for LLM memory systems by establishing a relative notion of truth. Through active probing to detect inconsistencies between retrieved memories and fresh observations, GLOVE enables memory-environment realignment by verifying and updating memory without access to ground-truth supervision or strong reliance on model introspection. We evaluate GLOVE on diverse benchmarks spanning web navigation, planning, and control, augmented with controlled environmental drifts that introduce non-stationarity beyond the original benchmark settings. Our results show that GLOVE substantially improves agent success rates, suggesting a robust pathway to cognitive agents capable of self-evolving.

arXiv|arxiv:2604.12102.title: Spatial Atlas: Compute-Grounded Reasoning for Spatial-Aware Research Agent Benchmarks
arXiv|arxiv:2604.12102.abstract: We describe compute-grounded reasoning (CGR), a design pattern in which code computes selected sub-problems from explicit intermediate representations before a language model answers. Spatial Atlas implements CGR as an Agent2Agent (A2A) server with a spatial question-answering handler and a machine-learning engineering handler. The spatial handler asks a language model to extract a scene graph, and code then fills in missing distances and checks the extracted safety rules. A separate benchmark driver can also run a strict metric bridge. It computes the gap for horizontal-gap questions from segmentation masks and a reconstructed point map, and it passes that gap to the answering model as a fact. The bridge returns a fixed unavailable answer when an evidence check fails, and it never falls back to model-estimated coordinates. The ML-engineering handler generates pipeline code, parses validation scores, and caps the number of repair and refinement passes. Its code execution is off by default. The repository also provides four run modes that can write label-free journals, a shuffled-image control mapping, and journal validators that reject label-bearing fields. We report one private label-free operational run in which four paths each wrote eight prediction rows with zero retries. Labels stayed sealed, and no score was computed, so this run establishes operational integrity only. We report no FieldWorkArena result because the benchmark data were not accessible. We also omit every performance, latency, and resource-use number that lacks a reproducible run artifact.

arXiv|arxiv:2601.21343.title: Self-Improving Training & Thinking
arXiv|arxiv:2601.21343.abstract: Large language models are classically trained in stages: pretraining on raw text followed by post-training for instruction following and reasoning. However, this separation creates a fundamental limitation: many desirable behaviors such as safety, factuality, overall generation quality, and reasoning ability are only added at a late stage, even though the patterns learned earlier strongly shape a model's capabilities. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new way to pretrain and mid-train models that incorporates these behaviors earlier. We utilize an existing strong, post-trained model to both rewrite data and to judge policy model rollouts, thus introducing thinking and reinforcement earlier in training. We further improve reasoning at all stages by introducing the concept of self-improving post-thinking: improving the model's reasoning and self-judging ability by reasoning after generation. In our experiments, we show these approaches can give strong gains across multiple axes.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.07964.title: Time-Indexed Skill Success Models for Latency-Aware Skill Selection and Timing in Dynamic Manipulation
arXiv|arxiv:2611.07964.abstract: Robots that manipulate moving objects act on observations that are outdated when the chosen skill starts, and the best skill can change within a few hundred milliseconds. Skill competence models, however, predict success for a launch at the moment of observation. We propose time-indexed skill success models, which predict whole-task success when a skill is launched after a given delay. Trained on rollouts branched at a grid of launch delays, they let a receding-horizon planner select both the skill and its launch time under fixed or random latency. In a MuJoCo study in which a UR5e captures a sliding puck with three skills, the planner exceeded a static competence model by 2.8 to 6.2 percentage points at 100 to 300 ms of latency, including when that model was evaluated on point or sampled forecasts of the launch state. Across five complete runs (three training seeds and two distribution shifts), all 80 paired 95% intervals against four baselines excluded zero. On delayed launches, the time-indexed model was calibrated (expected calibration error 0.009 against 0.239), and pausing the world during latency overstated success by up to 23 points. On a real UR5e that captures a rolling ball after 0.2 s of injected latency, a static model trained in a hardware-matched simulator predicted 99% success on a prespecified subset of 35 delayed launches that it rated at least 0.8. Of these, 63% succeeded (95% interval 46 to 77%), and the time-indexed model predicted 56%. In this single-skill, predictable regime, a matched physics-based forecast was also well calibrated.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: AutoML-Agent: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Full-Pipeline AutoML
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Automated machine learning (AutoML) accelerates AI development by automating tasks in the development pipeline, such as optimal model search and hyperparameter tuning. Existing AutoML systems often require technical expertise to set up complex tools, which is in general time-consuming and requires a large amount of human effort. Therefore, recent works have started exploiting large language models (LLM) to lessen such burden and increase the usability of AutoML frameworks via a natural language interface, allowing non-expert users to build their data-driven solutions. These methods, however, are usually designed only for a particular process in the AI development pipeline and do not efficiently use the inherent capacity of the LLMs. This paper proposes *AutoML-Agent*, a novel multi-agent framework tailored for full-pipeline AutoML, i.e., from data retrieval to model deployment. *AutoML-Agent* takes user's task descriptions, facilitates collaboration between specialized LLM agents, and delivers deployment-ready models. Unlike existing work, instead of devising a single plan, we introduce a retrieval-augmented planning strategy to enhance exploration to search for more optimal plans. We also decompose each plan into sub-tasks (e.g., data preprocessing and neural network design) each of which is solved by a specialized agent we build via prompting executing in parallel, making the search process more efficient. Moreover, we propose a multi-stage verification to verify executed results and guide the code generation LLM in implementing successful solutions. Extensive experiments on seven downstream tasks using fourteen datasets show that *AutoML-Agent* achieves a higher success rate in automating the full AutoML process, yielding systems with good performance throughout the diverse domains.

CVF|https://openaccess.thecvf.com/conten.abstract: Multimodal learning often grapples with the challenge of low-quality data, which predominantly manifests as two facets: modality imbalance and noisy corruption. While these issues are often studied in isolation, we argue that they share a common root in the predictive uncertainty towards the reliability of individual modalities and instances during learning. In this paper, we propose a unified framework, termed Conformal Predictive Self-Calibration (CPSC), which leverages conformal prediction to equip the model with the ability to perform self-guided calibration on-the-fly. The core of our proposed CPSC lies in a novel self-calibrating training loop that seamlessly integrates two key modules: (1) Representation Self-Calibration, which decomposes unimodal features into components, selectively fuses the most robust ones identified by a conformal predictor to enhance feature resilience. (2) Gradient Self-Calibration, which recalibrates the gradient flow during backpropagation based on instance-wise reliability scores, steering the optimization towards more trustworthy directions. Furthermore, we also devise a self-update strategy for the conformal predictor to ensure the entire system co-evolves consistently throughout the training process. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets under both imbalanced and noisy settings demonstrate that our CPSC framework consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/XunCHN/CPSC.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.24975.title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
arXiv|arxiv:2611.24975.abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: MemGen: Weaving Generative Latent Memory for Self-Evolving Agents
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Agent memory shapes how Large Language Model (LLM)-powered agents, akin to the human brain, progressively refine themselves through environment interactions. Existing paradigms remain constrained: parametric memory forcibly adjusts model parameters, and retrieval-based memory externalizes experience into structured databases, yet neither captures the fluid interweaving of reasoning and memory that underlies human cognition. To address this gap, we propose MemGen, a dynamic generative memory framework that equips agents with a human-esque cognitive faculty. It consists of a \textit{memory trigger}, which monitors the agent’s reasoning state to decide explicit memory invocation, and a \textit{memory weaver}, which takes the agent's current state as stimulus to construct a latent token sequence as machine-native memory to enrich its reasoning. In this way, MemGen enables agents to recall and augment latent memory throughout reasoning, producing a tightly interwoven cycle of memory and cognition. Extensive experiments across eight benchmarks show that MemGen surpasses leading external memory systems such as ExpeL and AWM by up to $38.22\\%$, exceeds GRPO by up to $13.44\\%$, and exhibits strong cross-domain generalization ability. More importantly, we find that without explicit supervision, MemGen spontaneously evolves distinct human-like memory faculties, including planning memory, procedural memory, and working memory, suggesting an emergent trajectory toward more naturalistic forms of machine cognition.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) benchmarks in NLP use number-right scoring (accuracy), but in educational testing, the scoring scheme—the combination of the response mode models follow and the rule for grading responses—is a key design choice that dictates which abilities to reward. arXiv|arxiv:2611.34211.title: Compute-Aware Submodular Online Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
arXiv|arxiv:2611.34211.abstract: This paper studies policy learning for cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems, where submodular utilities model diminishing marginal returns due to overlapping agent contributions. While standard methods evaluate every candidate action to update the policy, this may incur an excessive computational cost online. Hence, we impose a budget on these evaluations and analytically study the effect of query budget on online learning. Our algorithm samples a prescribed number of agent-action pairs and applies inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, yielding an unbiased gradient estimate of the expected stage utility for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. We derive a $1/2$-approximate regret bound that elegantly splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies, quantified by their KL divergence, and a query-dependent feedback term. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show that our approach retains high performance with significantly less computation online.

arXiv|arxiv:2602.19458.abstract: Multi-agent decision pipelines can outperform single agent workflows when complementarity holds, i.e., different agents bring unique information to inform a final decision. arXiv|arxiv:2609.37298.title: Scaling Full Conformal Image Classifiers
arXiv|arxiv:2609.37298.abstract: Conformal prediction provides set-valued predictions with distribution-free coverage guarantees, making it attractive for high-stakes image classification. However, split conformal prediction is data-inefficient, while full conformal prediction (FCP), despite its stronger statistical efficiency, is computationally prohibitive at scale because it requires candidate-specific model refits at test time. We address this limitation by leveraging zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) to guide scalable FCP in large label spaces. We introduce Targeted Full Conformal Prediction (T-FCP), which uses a lightweight inductive conformal predictor to prune unlikely labels and applies FCP only to the remaining candidates, reducing computation while retaining the formal guarantee of the combined conformal procedure. We further propose Stabilized Online LDA (SO-LDA), an efficient VLM adaptation solver based on rank-one inverse-covariance updates. Across multiple benchmarks, including ImageNet, T-FCP enables practical full-conformal image classification with modest test-time overhead, yielding efficient prediction sets and more stable empirical coverage than split conformal alternatives.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.34956.title: Decision Model Factory: Building Specialized Sovereign Decision Models
arXiv|arxiv:2610.34956.abstract: Decision needs vary with each application, language, and deployment environment. The Decision Model Factory turns those needs into specialized, sovereign models on demand. A brief recipe guides the training, calibration, verification, and evaluation of a selected backbone, delivering a deployable decision model under the operator's control. The same workflow creates a new specialist whenever the requirements change. Across Japanese decision tasks, compact deployment, and long-context passage ranking, five factory-built models improve upon their backbones; three surpass the strongest results in a fixed public Japanese benchmark comparison. A dedicated runner computes only permitted-answer probabilities and reuses shared context, more than doubling serving speed on matched multi-question workloads with essentially unchanged decision scores. Together, the factory and runner make fast, task-specific decision models practical to build and deploy whenever needed.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.28811.title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems
arXiv|arxiv:2610.28811.abstract: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.

PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v337/.title: Reliable Conformal Prediction for Ordinal Classification Using the Ranked Probability Score
PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v337/.abstract: Ordinal classification (OC) arises in high-stakes domains such as medicine and finance, where uncertainty quantification must account for the severity of ordinal errors. Conformal prediction ({CP}) provides distribution-free prediction sets with marginal coverage guarantees; however, its practical effectiveness depends critically on the choice of nonconformity function. We introduce a {CP} method for ordinal classification based on the ranked probability score ({RPS}), a proper scoring rule defined over cumulative predictive distributions. Although it reflects ordinal risk quite naturally, it has largely been neglected in conformal ordinal prediction (COP). When used as a measure of nonconformity, {RPS} yields median-centered contiguous prediction sets by construction. The method is model-agnostic, supports both assessed and grouped ordered categorical outcomes, and permits efficient implementation compared to greedy interval selection procedures. Across multiple ordinal image and tabular datasets, {RPS}-based {CP} produces contiguous prediction sets and strikes a favorable balance between prediction set width and the magnitude of ordinal miscoverage relative to existing {CP} methods.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Policy-Level Exploration for Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: In multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), agents must not only discover high-reward behaviours but also reliably reproduce coordinated behaviours over time. A fundamental challenge arises from a mismatch between action-level stochastic exploration and temporally extended coordination. To address this issue, we propose a policy-level exploration framework with Deterministic Action Execution (DAE) for MARL, which shifts locally random action exploration to temporally extended policy selection via an option-based exploration mechanism. Specifically, at each time step, each agent selects a policy from a shared policy set\textemdash comprising one exploitation policy and multiple exploration policies\textemdash using a learned option policy, and actions are executed deterministically conditioned on the selected policy. By maintaining deterministic execution under temporally extended policy selection, DAE facilitates temporally coordinated behaviours across multiple time steps. Comprehensive experiments on five multi-agent tasks\textemdash Predator Prey, StarCraft II micro management challenge (SMAC), SMACv2, Google Research Football, and Multi-Agent Coordination benchmark (MACO)\textemdash demonstrate that DAE outperforms mainstream baselines in terms of sample efficiency and final learning performance.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.29912.title: SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
arXiv|arxiv:2611.29912.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability. CVF|https://openaccess.thecvf.com/conten.abstract: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for ensuring the reliability of machine learning models deployed in real-world autonomous systems. However, existing approaches typically quantify task-level output prediction uncertainty without considering epistemic uncertainty at the multimodal feature fusion level, leading to sub-optimal outcomes. Additionally, popular uncertainty quantification methods, e.g., Bayesian approximations, remain challenging to deploy in practice due to high computational costs in training and inference. In this paper, we propose HyperDUM, a novel deterministic uncertainty method (DUM) that efficiently quantifies feature-level epistemic uncertainty by leveraging hyperdimensional computing. arXiv|arxiv:2610.41132.title: When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2610.41132.abstract: The EU Platform Work Directive, to be transposed by December 2026, requires ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker's behaviour affects them. Such rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to let one decide for them. We compare two main families of rebalancing policy once their rules are public: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent maximizing its own net income, given no rules (N) or the rules at the directive's level of detail (L). We test two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, which understand the rules equally well, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. With the rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the effects differ by policy. For the platform, disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for moves drivers used to make for free, while A's profit is unchanged; the two policies, which tie on profit under full compliance, end 6.1% apart. For drivers, disclosure raises income in the small model under both policies and LLMs; for users, it raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In Manhattan, self-interested drivers also make A a win-win-win against full compliance, raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each. Rebalancing policies that perform equally well under full compliance can thus show opposite results under mandatory disclosure. The study offers a framework to evaluate such policies under the new requirement and is, to our knowledge, the first to do so with LLM agents.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: We present a differentiable optimization framework for multi-agent coordination. An input is decomposed into overlapping local views, each processed by an agent that solves a convex subproblem parameterized by a neural encoder. arXiv|arxiv:2611.00676.title: Smooth bounding box for object detection
arXiv|arxiv:2611.00676.abstract: Deep learning-based object detection models are highly dependent on the quality of annotated training data. However, large-scale datasets often contain inevitable label noise, with bounding box localization errors being a prevalent and impactful form in object detection. While label noise handling techniques are well-studied for image classification, their adaptation to the more complex problem of bounding box errors remains underexplored. To address this, we propose a novel Smooth Bounding Box (SBB) strategy to mitigate the adverse effects of bounding box annotation inaccuracies. Our key insight is that annotation errors are often linked to annotator factors rather than specific image content, allowing for a statistical correction approach. Based on object size distribution within datasets, we implement the SBB strategy through two methods: 1) Global Scaling Correction (GSC), which applies a uniform scaling factor to estimate and correct a global average error; and 2) Interval Scaling Correction (ISC), which categorizes objects by size into intervals and estimates a dedicated correction factor for each, enabling more precise, fine-grained calibration. For efficient optimization of multiple parameters in ISC, we design a tailored model fine-tuning strategy. Furthermore, we introduce a Normalized Residual Fluctuation (NRF) metric to quantitatively assess the smoothing effect and training stability. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently enhances detection accuracy across various model architectures. Both GSC and ISC achieve significant performance improvements over strong baselines, including the latest YOLOv11n, without adding inference overhead. The codes are available at https://github.com/Acui001/SBB.git.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.36557.title: QESChunker: A Single Objective Unifies Overlapping and Non-Overlapping Chunking for RAG
arXiv|arxiv:2610.36557.abstract: Chunking is a fundamental preprocessing step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), yet most existing chunkers rely primarily on heuristics. We introduce the Question--Evidence-Supervised Chunker (QESChunker), to our knowledge the first method for constructing static chunk indices from question--evidence supervision. QESChunker constructs document-specific chunk indices by optimizing over human-annotated or LLM-generated question--evidence pairs, without access to held-out test queries. We formulate non-overlapping and overlapping index construction through a unified question--evidence utility-maximization objective, turning chunking into a supervised combinatorial optimization problem. Under the non-overlap constraint, the objective decomposes over chunks and can be optimized exactly in polynomial time by dynamic programming. When overlap is allowed, the objective becomes monotone submodular; exact optimization is NP-hard, but our greedy achieves a $(1-1/\sqrt{e})$-approximation. Across two self-constructed and three public datasets, both variants outperform existing chunking methods in complete-evidence recall in nearly all evaluated settings, under the same overlap regime and a fixed hybrid retriever. These results recast chunking as supervised, budget-aware index construction for evidence retrieval.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Grammars of Formal Uncertainty: When to Trust LLMs in Automated Reasoning Tasks
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show remarkable promise for democratizing automated reasoning by generating formal specifications. However, a fundamental tension exists: LLMs are probabilistic, while formal verification demands deterministic guarantees. This paper addresses this epistemological gap by comprehensively investigating failure modes and uncertainty quantification (UQ) in LLM-generated formal artifacts. Our systematic evaluation of five frontier LLMs reveals Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) based autoformalization's domain-specific impact on accuracy (from +34.8\% on logical tasks to -44.5\% on factual ones), with known UQ techniques like the entropy of token probabilities failing to identify these errors. We introduce a probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG) framework to model LLM outputs, yielding a refined uncertainty taxonomy. We find uncertainty signals are task-dependent (e.g., grammar entropy for logic, AUROC>0.93). Finally, a lightweight fusion of these signals enables selective verification, drastically reducing errors (14-100\%) with minimal abstention, transforming LLM-driven formalization into a reliable engineering discipline.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.09489.title: Goldsmith: Gold-Loss-Guided Definition Optimization with an Agentic Annotation Harness
arXiv|arxiv:2610.09489.abstract: Many annotation projects begin before experts have a stable guideline or enough labels to train a task-specific model. We present Goldsmith, an agentic pipeline that turns a small gold set---expert-annotated calibration examples representing the intended task boundaries---into a reusable structured annotation definition. Goldsmith treats this definition as a trainable textual object. Candidate definitions are run on the same gold examples and scored with an executable structured loss, while the output schema, formatting, retrieval, repair, judging, and human review remain in an external harness. A large language model (LLM) editor converts the highest-loss failures into textual-gradient revisions, which are accepted only when the measured loss decreases. In prompt-optimization comparisons, Goldsmith improves over direct rewriting, OPRO, APE, and PromptBreeder under matched evaluation protocols. The resulting definition also improves downstream annotation when combined with retrieval, score-based routing, and human review across typed span, pair-level relation, and fixed-trigger event-argument tasks. These results show that scarce expert supervision can support both task-definition learning and scalable annotation.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.20939.title: MAI-Gym: An Open All-in-One Platform for GUI Agent Evaluation and RL Training across Mobile and Computer Environments
arXiv|arxiv:2610.20939.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has driven rapid progress in mathematics, coding, and tool use, but scaling this success to GUI agents remains challenging due to the high cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks. We introduce MAI-Gym, an open all-in-one platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments. Through a shared rollout pipeline, MAI-Gym ensures consistent agent behavior across evaluation and training, supports ten established benchmarks, and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances. Beyond scalable infrastructure, MAI-Gym enables automated synthesis of diverse GUI applications and challenging tasks, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers. Using MAI-Gym, we train MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open GUI agents under 10B parameters: 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified. Importantly, RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a phys- ical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. We release the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint to support repro- ducible research and further advances in scalable GUI agent training.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.32686.title: CAPTA: Identifying LLMs Behind AI Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2611.32686.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents access remote services through tools to complete user tasks, often via API calls. In this setting, a remote service may want to identify the backend LLM of an agent to launch model-specific attacks, including prompt injection or selective delivery of manipulated content. However, the service cannot directly query the backend model and must instead collect observable responses through its interactions with the agent, making identification challenging. In this paper, we present Completely Automated Preference Test to tell LLMs Apart (CAPTA), a model identification approach inspired by CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), which distinguishes humans from automated programs. CAPTA presents multiple-choice questions as verification challenges, using differences in models' selection preferences to identify the backend LLM. It selects questions based on cross-model option-generation diversity and uses LLM-guided search to optimize their option sets. Our evaluation shows that CAPTA achieves 99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions across 25 LLMs from 10 model families. We further evaluate CAPTA with four widely used agents and seven representative LLMs, achieving 99.7% mean identification accuracy across all 28 agent-LLM combinations with 30 submitted answers.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Understanding how and why large language models (LLMs) fail is becoming a central challenge as models rapidly evolve and static evaluations fall behind. While automated probing has been enabled by dynamic test generation, existing approaches often discover isolated failure cases, lack principled control over exploration, and provide limited insight into the underlying structure of model weaknesses. We propose ProbeLLM, a benchmark-agnostic automated probing framework that elevates weakness discovery from individual failures to structured failure modes. ProbeLLM formulates probing as a hierarchical Monte Carlo Tree Search, explicitly allocating limited probing budgets between global exploration of new failure regions and local refinement of recurring error patterns. By restricting probing to verifiable test cases and leveraging tool-augmented generation and verification, ProbeLLM grounds failure discovery in reliable evidence. Discovered failures are further consolidated into interpretable failure modes via failure-aware embeddings and boundary-aware induction. Across diverse benchmarks and LLMs, ProbeLLM reveals substantially broader, cleaner, and more fine-grained failure landscapes than static benchmarks and prior automated methods, supporting a shift from case-centric evaluation toward principled weakness discovery

arXiv|arxiv:2610.19906.title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Diagnostic Test for LLM Chemical Prediction
arXiv|arxiv:2610.19906.abstract: LLMs have achieved strong performance on chemical prediction benchmarks. However, existing evaluation methods typically provide target entity identity information directly, making it difficult to determine whether model predictions arise from transferable structure-property reasoning capabilities or rely on target-related contextual information or memory retrieval. We propose the Identity-Blinded Reasoning Diagnostic framework to evaluate chemical prediction models when target entity identity information is hidden. In this framework, the target is no longer directly defined by its entity identity, but instead by a known source entity and an explicit structural edit operation. This setting preserves the information required to determine the target while reducing the opportunity for models to access target identity cues. We evaluate this framework across six tasks spanning odor prediction, molecular property prediction, retrosynthesis, and reaction yield prediction. The results show that models generally achieve better prediction performance when source and target entity properties are consistent. Providing explicit source entity labels further strengthens this dependence. Moreover, while keeping the target entity, structural change, and ground-truth label unchanged, replacing only the source entity label causes some model predictions to systematically shift toward the substituted source labels. These results indicate that high benchmark accuracy in chemical prediction tasks does not necessarily imply that LLMs possess reliable structure-property reasoning capabilities. Our diagnostic framework provides a controlled evaluation approach for testing whether models can genuinely update predictions according to entity changes. The framework can be extended to other AI for Science tasks, particularly those where targets can be defined through transformations of known entities.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.06597.title: A trust layer for fast pedestal-stability surrogates: calibrated error bars, out-of-distribution alarms and few-shot recalibration
arXiv|arxiv:2611.06597.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates of linear peeling-ballooning stability now run in milliseconds, but they are mostly deployed as point estimators: they do not say how wrong they may be, or when a query lies outside what they were trained on. For a fusion company designing a new device, every equilibrium of interest is outside the training data of existing surrogates, so this is the case that matters. We describe a model-agnostic trust layer for stability surrogates, made of conformal error bars, out-of-distribution alarms that route doubtful cases to the physics code, and recalibration from a few simulations of a new design, and we test it with pre-registered hypotheses. On a large public dataset of JET-like equilibria with ideal-MHD growth rates, the error bars hold their nominal coverage in distribution and fall short under a shift in plasma shape; a few dozen simulations of the new shape, or routing the cases the alarms flag, restore it. On resistive BOUT++ surrogates, the bars stay calibrated on held-out runs, the alarm flags tokamaks absent from training, and a scenario scan is screened in seconds instead of hours. Across equilibria from the SPARC library and the DIII-D coil set, a surrogate trained on our own graded BOUT++ labels beats the baseline on unseen equilibria, while a surrogate trained elsewhere ranks the same cases backwards and its alarm declines them. Building our own neural-operator surrogate, the harness exposed two input defects whose fix closed its gap to a simple network. For every surrogate tested, the trust layer keeps coverage near target, with a bar width set by that surrogate's own error. Not every pre-registered hypothesis held, and we report those results and the limits of all of them.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.21125.title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
arXiv|arxiv:2610.21125.abstract: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.

PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/.title: Position: Agentic Safety is an Epistemic Property, Not a Behavioral One
PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/.abstract: Contemporary AI safety spans pre-training interventions, post-training alignment, deployment-time controls, monitoring, and red-teaming. These methods are necessary, but they primarily certify snapshots of system behavior. As AI systems become more capable, dynamic, embodied, and self-improving, this snapshot view becomes incomplete: safety depends not only on whether a system behaves acceptably now, but whether it remains correctable as it learns, adapts, acts, and modifies itself over time. This paper argues that safety should therefore be treated as an epistemic property of the evolving learner, not merely a behavioral property of the current policy. We introduce teachability as the capacity to preserve future corrective leverage under bounded human, institutional, or environmental intervention. We argue that advanced systems can retain visible competence while eroding the representational, algorithmic, or meta-decision conditions needed for future correction. Safe advanced AI systems must not only behave acceptably now; they must remain teachable later.
